aggressive_definition: Advanced incident prostate cancer, defined as Gleason score ≥7 or stage III or IV.
aggressive_definition_excerpt: advanced prostate cancer (i.e., Gleason score > or = 7 or stage III or IV)
study_design: Prospective cohort analysis of men in the screening arm of the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial.
cohort_total_n_excerpt: We identified 1338 cases of prostate cancer among 29 361 men during up to 8 years of follow-up.
reason: The abstract reports incident total prostate cancer during follow-up and separately analyzes incident advanced prostate cancer defined by grade or stage.

estimate_classifications.endpoint_excerpt: However, among current and recent (i.e., within the previous 10 years) smokers, decreasing risks of advanced prostate cancer (i.e., Gleason score > or = 7 or stage III or IV) were associated with increasing dose (RR for > 400 IU/day versus none = 0.29, 95% CI = 0.12 to 0.68; Ptrend = .01) and duration (RR for > or = 10 years of use versus none = 0.30, 95% CI = 0.09 to 0.96; Ptrend = .01) of supplemental vitamin E use.
estimate_classifications.reason: The estimate explicitly pertains to advanced incident prostate cancer among current and recent smokers.

estimate_classifications.endpoint_excerpt: Supplemental beta-carotene intake at a dose level of at least 2000 microg/day was associated with decreased prostate cancer risk in men with low (below the median of 4129 microg/day) dietary beta-carotene intake (RR = 0.52, 95% CI = 0.33 to 0.81).
estimate_classifications.reason: The estimate is for prostate cancer overall, with no aggressive-stage or grade restriction stated.

estimate_classifications.endpoint_excerpt: Overall, there was no association between prostate cancer risk and dietary or supplemental intake of vitamin E, beta-carotene, or vitamin C.
estimate_classifications.reason: The qualitative vitamin C result pertains to overall prostate cancer risk, not specifically aggressive disease.
